clusters.name: Data Ingestion Mode
clusters.description: The axis varies how raw features and datasets enter ML workflows, distinguishing batch, streaming, and organizational storage arrangements from later preparation decisions.

relations.rationale: Ingested data must be available before feature preparation and validation can occur.

values.label: External-source ingestion
values.description: Features are collected from systems or sources outside the ML pipeline.

values.label: ETL-based ingestion
values.description: Batch-oriented extract, transform, and load processes bring features into the workflow.

values.label: Streaming ingestion
values.description: Features enter the workflow continuously through streaming mechanisms.

values.label: Centralized consistent storage
values.description: Accessible data is retained in a consistent structure, ideally in one centralized location.

clusters.name: Feature Preparation and Validation
clusters.description: The axis varies how raw data becomes trustworthy model input through transformation, profiling, validation, visualization, and feature engineering.

relations.rationale: Prepared and validated features are prerequisites for dependable model training.
Preparation choices determine how ingested data is transformed for downstream learning.

values.label: Dedicated feature engineering pipeline
values.description: A distinct pipeline selects, transforms, combines, and prepares raw data before algorithm use.

values.label: Feature preparation tooling
values.description: Spark, Python, or database capabilities implement feature analysis and transformation.

values.label: Metadata and distribution profiling
values.description: Attribute metadata, value distributions, and visualizations are documented to understand dataset structure.

values.label: User-defined dataset validation
values.description: Custom routines detect inconsistencies, incorrect associations, missing values, and other data errors.

values.label: Additional-data feedback loop
values.description: Insufficient data sends the workflow back to ingestion to acquire useful additional information.

clusters.name: Training Execution Strategy
clusters.description: The axis varies when, where, and how models are trained, including batch versus incremental execution, triggering, scheduling, and parallelization.

relations.rationale: Training execution produces candidate models that must subsequently be evaluated and tested.
Training schedules, parallelism, and execution modes constrain required serving and operational infrastructure.

values.label: Offline batch training
values.description: Training runs as an offline process rather than during prediction requests.

values.label: Real-time online learning
values.description: The model updates continuously or incrementally while operating on incoming data.

values.label: Time- and event-triggered training
values.description: Schedulers, calendar events, messages, monitoring events, or data and code changes initiate training.

values.label: Criticality-dependent training schedule
values.description: Training frequency varies according to application criticality, from multiple times daily to daily execution.

values.label: Parallel candidate-model training
values.description: Multiple algorithms, parameter configurations, or candidate models train concurrently.

values.label: Data-partitioned model replicas
values.description: Data is partitioned and a model replica trains on each partition.

values.label: Model-partitioned parameter updates
values.description: The model is partitioned so separate workers update different parameter subsets.

values.label: Checkpointed training partitions
values.description: Training partitions use checkpoints and retry or failover mechanisms after transient failures.

values.label: Stochastic-gradient incremental training
values.description: Stochastic gradient descent provides the optimization routine for incremental online learning.

clusters.name: Model Evaluation and Testing
clusters.description: The axis varies how candidate models, training behavior, pipeline integrity, and production readiness are assessed before release.

relations.rationale: Evaluation evidence and test results support decisions to promote model artifacts through lifecycle stages.
Serving a model requires evidence that its quality and runtime behavior meet acceptance criteria.

values.label: Held-out-data evaluation
values.description: Performance is measured on data not used during training to assess generalization.

values.label: Pluggable evaluator library
values.description: Multiple evaluation metrics can be combined or exchanged through a flexible evaluator library.

values.label: Evaluation-subset model selection
values.description: The best candidate is selected by comparing performance against true values in an evaluation dataset.

values.label: Hyperparameter optimization and regularization
values.description: Iterative optimization and regularization refine candidate models before final selection.

values.label: Deterministic reproducible training
values.description: Training is designed to produce identical models from identical data and controlled randomness.

values.label: Automated end-to-end pipeline testing
values.description: The complete data, training, and model pipeline is regularly executed and checked before production.

values.label: Validation-set regression thresholds
values.description: Quality thresholds detect gradual or sudden degradation across model versions.

values.label: Canary serving validation
values.description: A model is tested in a production-like serving environment using realistic data before full service.

values.label: Diff-testing against previous models
values.description: Comparing new models directly with previously built models is explicitly discouraged because maintenance is difficult.

clusters.name: Prediction Serving Interaction
clusters.description: The axis varies the temporal and communication contract by which predictions are requested, completed, delivered, and retrieved.

relations.rationale: The selected interaction contract determines serving components, routing, storage, and scaling requirements.
Serving interactions commonly depend on model versions and lifecycle states recorded in governance systems.

values.label: Synchronous online serving
values.description: A caller submits a request and receives a prediction during the request interaction.

values.label: Asynchronous offline serving
values.description: Large collections are scored as batch jobs, with results retrieved after completion.

values.label: Push-based score delivery
values.description: Completed predictions are delivered to the caller through an independent notification.

values.label: Polling-based score retrieval
values.description: The caller periodically checks a low-latency store for completed predictions.

values.label: Broker-based completion notification
values.description: A message broker signals completion of offline scoring before consumers fetch results.

values.label: Model-version request routing
values.description: Requests identify a model version and a router directs them to the corresponding model.

values.label: Cached offline predictions
values.description: Precomputed predictions are cached to reduce access latency for repeated or relevant requests.

clusters.name: Serving Architecture and Scalability
clusters.description: The axis varies the structural deployment pattern used to host, scale, isolate, and accelerate model prediction services.

relations.rationale: Architecture choices restrict which prediction interaction patterns and latency targets can be supported.
Serving architectures are commonly packaged and promoted through automated delivery pipelines.

values.label: Separate model and API deployment
values.description: The model and feature-retrieval or invocation APIs operate as distinct serving components.

values.label: Containerized prediction microservice
values.description: A prediction model is packaged and deployed as a containerized microservice.

values.label: Clustered queue-backed serving
values.description: Online serving runs across a cluster behind a queue for load balancing, throughput, and low latency.

values.label: Parallel stateless prediction pipelines
values.description: Multiple stateless prediction pipelines scale horizontally to accommodate load.

values.label: In-memory feature store
values.description: Input features are kept in a low-read-latency in-memory store for online prediction.

values.label: Key-value model store
values.description: Models and parameters are stored in a key-value system to improve serving performance.

values.label: Microservice architecture
values.description: Clearly separated product components are independently served as microservices.

values.label: Monolithic architecture
values.description: Tightly integrated components with heavily shared complex data access use a monolithic structure.

values.label: Hybrid microservice-monolith architecture
values.description: Microservice and monolithic structures are combined when both separation and shared integration are needed.

values.label: Universal default monolith
values.description: Treating the standard monolith as suitable for every situation is explicitly rejected.

clusters.name: ML Delivery Automation
clusters.description: The axis varies the degree and mechanism of automation for experimentation, testing, orchestration, training, deployment, and infrastructure operations.

relations.rationale: Automated delivery creates lifecycle events, versions, and promotion records that governance systems must track.
Automation enables recurring operation and monitoring rather than isolated manual model releases.

values.label: Manual RAD pipeline execution
values.description: Preparation, training, validation, and testing are performed manually with exploratory tools such as notebooks.

values.label: Pull-request-triggered experiments
values.description: Code changes submitted through pull requests automatically launch experiment execution.

values.label: Automated CI/CD pipeline
values.description: Code, data, models, and pipelines are automatically built, tested, and deployed.

values.label: Event-triggered model deployment
values.description: Data, code, monitoring, messages, or calendar events trigger training and deployment workflows.

values.label: Interdependent-task orchestration
values.description: Feature engineering, training, and prediction tasks are scheduled and coordinated across compute infrastructure.

values.label: End-to-end MLOps automation
values.description: Integration, testing, release, deployment, infrastructure management, and training are automated as one lifecycle.

values.label: MLOps platform automation
values.description: An end-to-end platform automates technical tasks and reduces operational bottlenecks at scale.

clusters.name: Model Governance and Lineage
clusters.description: The axis varies how models, code, data, metadata, versions, lifecycle stages, and deployment eligibility are recorded and controlled.

relations.rationale: Evaluation and testing produce evidence that is attached to candidate models and informs promotion.
Governance records are created and advanced through automated delivery workflows.
Approved versions and lifecycle stages constrain which models can serve prediction requests.

values.label: Self-contained model artifacts
values.description: Artifacts contain the preprocessing and prediction components required to generate results.

values.label: Model-code-data lineage
values.description: Relationships among models, training code, training data, and test data are tracked.

values.label: Centralized model registry
values.description: Production candidates are published and managed in a central registry or hub.

values.label: Published-model metadata catalog
values.description: The registry records identifiers, locations, datasets, metrics, and system or business metadata.

values.label: Model version tracking
values.description: Versions and their publication dates are recorded for change management.

values.label: Lifecycle-stage promotion
values.description: Artifacts are explicitly marked for development, staging, production, or archival stages.

values.label: Governance and audit metadata
values.description: Registry records support auditability and regulatory requirements.

values.label: Shadow-mode model testing
values.description: Candidate model changes are evaluated alongside production behavior before or during deployment.

clusters.name: Operational Monitoring Strategy
clusters.description: The axis varies how deployed models are observed, reviewed, and checked for health, quality degradation, failures, and business impact.

relations.rationale: Operational monitoring extends pre-release quality checks into production and can trigger retraining or rollback.
Monitoring findings can trigger or constrain automated retraining, testing, and deployment workflows.
Monitoring practices depend on the infrastructure and access controls available for production operation.

values.label: End-to-end lifecycle monitoring
values.description: Models, infrastructure, and all ML construction and operation steps are monitored continuously.

values.label: Data-scientist-led monitoring
values.description: The model creator personally collects feedback, iterates, and supervises the model after deployment.

values.label: Periodic model health checks
values.description: Teams revisit deployed models at regular intervals for basic health assessment.

values.label: User-reported issue detection
values.description: Users identify failures and problems, after which the team responds reactively.

values.label: Custom monitoring dashboard
values.description: Important models use internally built dashboards for dedicated operational observation.

values.label: Failure-driven monitoring checks
values.description: Custom checks are added incrementally after operational failures occur.

values.label: Separated model and business KPI reporting
values.description: Operational model metrics and business KPI reports are maintained in separate views or silos.

values.label: Partial monitoring coverage
values.description: Only a minority of deployed models receive monitoring, leaving substantial operational blind spots.

values.label: Hosted model-serving infrastructure
values.description: Models are hosted and maintained on dedicated infrastructure after deployment.

values.label: Hybrid cloud and on-premises infrastructure
values.description: Cloud services coexist with on-premises systems to accommodate sensitive workloads and existing infrastructure.

values.label: On-premises sensitive-data retention
values.description: Private or sensitive data remains on company-controlled servers to reduce exposure risk.

values.label: Enterprise-standard RStudio platform
values.description: An organization mandates RStudio Server as the standard data-science development platform.

values.label: Mandatory R-language constraint
values.description: Organizational guidelines require data-science projects to use R.

values.label: Notebook-based prototyping
values.description: Data scientists prototype with notebooks despite an enterprise-provided platform.

values.label: Model access authentication
values.description: Authentication restricts model use to authorized parties.

values.label: Hybrid infrastructure management complexity
values.description: Operating cloud and on-premises environments together creates additional management complexity.

values.label: Sensitive-data exposure risk
values.description: A vulnerability affecting private data can have catastrophic consequences and motivates infrastructure isolation.

relations.rationale: Evaluation evidence and test results support decisions to promote model artifacts through lifecycle stages.
Serving a model requires evidence that its quality and runtime behavior meet acceptance criteria.

values.label: Held-out-data evaluation
values.description: Performance is measured on data not used during training to assess generalization.

values.label: Pluggable evaluator library
values.description: Multiple evaluation metrics can be combined or exchanged through a flexible evaluator library.

values.label: Evaluation-subset model selection
values.description: The best candidate is selected by comparing performance against true values in an evaluation dataset.

values.label: Fairness and inclusion testing
values.description: Candidate models are tested for fairness, bias, inclusion, and protected-category effects before release.

values.label: Business-impact-aligned evaluation
values.description: Model metrics are evaluated together with business outcomes such as revenue or engagement.

values.label: Out-of-fold prediction blending
values.description: Combining out-of-fold candidate predictions to form the final prediction pipeline.

values.label: Multi-criteria operational evaluation
values.description: Evaluation considers stability, ethics, fairness, explainability, user experience, and edge cases beyond error alone.

values.label: Single-objective error minimization
values.description: Considering one error objective instead of broader operational criteria was rejected for model assessment.

values.label: Model interpretability instrumentation
values.description: Interpretability mechanisms explain model results for users, governance, and regulatory needs.

values.label: Ground-truth-limited precision and recall
values.description: Inaccurate labels impose an upper bound on achievable model precision and recall.

values.label: Heuristic baseline model
values.description: Use simple hand-crafted rules as a reference model for evaluating later ML models.

clusters.name: Ground Truth and Labeling Strategy

relations.rationale: Evaluation evidence and test results support decisions to promote model artifacts through lifecycle stages.
Serving a model requires evidence that its quality and runtime behavior meet acceptance criteria.

values.label: Ground-truth construction and label separation
values.description: Practitioners construct accurate labels and preserve distinctions between materially different outcome categories.

values.label: Chargeback-type separation for modeling
values.description: Separating chargeback types as a modeling ground-truth strategy was explicitly rejected.

values.label: Web-based manual labeling
values.description: Use a web application to support human creation of ground-truth labels.

values.label: Outsourced manual labeling
values.description: Use an external labeling service to create ground-truth labels.

clusters.name: Model Optimization Strategy
clusters.description: Which search, tuning, regularization, and optimization strategy should select or improve model configurations?

relations.rationale: Evaluation evidence and test results support decisions to promote model artifacts through lifecycle stages.
Serving a model requires evidence that its quality and runtime behavior meet acceptance criteria.

values.label: Hyperparameter optimization and regularization
values.description: Iterative optimization and regularization refine candidate models before final selection.

values.label: Manual deep-learning hyperparameter tuning
values.description: Manually exploring deep-learning hyperparameters without automated search.

values.label: Expanded deep-learning hyperparameter search space
values.description: Growth in the number of hyperparameters that makes exhaustive manual search impractical.

values.label: Reduced hyperparameter-search burden
values.description: Reduced data-scientist effort resulting from automated hyperparameter optimization.

values.label: Neural architecture search
values.description: Automated search selects neural architectures using defined spaces, metrics, and search algorithms.

values.label: Ecological-cost optimization
values.description: Model optimization accounts for computational carbon footprint as an objective.

values.label: Model optimization objective selection
values.description: Selecting the performance criterion or error type that model optimization prioritizes.

values.label: Automated algorithm and model selection
values.description: Automation evaluates multiple algorithms or models to select a suitable candidate during training.

values.label: Heuristic rule complexity
values.description: Rule-based fraud heuristics become unwieldy as fraud vectors grow more complex and evolve.

clusters.name: Pre-release Validation
clusters.description: Which testing and release checks should establish pipeline integrity and production readiness?

relations.rationale: Evaluation evidence and test results support decisions to promote model artifacts through lifecycle stages.
Serving a model requires evidence that its quality and runtime behavior meet acceptance criteria.

values.label: Automated end-to-end pipeline testing
values.description: The complete data, training, and model pipeline is regularly executed and checked before production.

values.label: Validation-set regression thresholds
values.description: Quality thresholds detect gradual or sudden degradation across model versions.

values.label: Canary serving validation
values.description: A model is tested in a production-like serving environment using realistic data before full service.

values.label: Diff-testing against previous models
values.description: Comparing new models directly with previously built models is explicitly discouraged because maintenance is difficult.

values.label: Competing-model production testing
values.description: Multiple candidate models receive split production traffic for comparative performance evaluation.

values.label: Traffic-splitting and data-collection complexity
values.description: Comparative production testing increases operational complexity while traffic is divided and evidence accumulates.

clusters.name: Prediction Serving Interaction
clusters.description: The axis varies the temporal and communication contract by which predictions are requested, completed, delivered, and retrieved.

relations.rationale: The selected interaction contract determines serving components, routing, storage, and scaling requirements.
The selected interaction contract determines serving components, routing, storage, and scaling requirements.
The selected interaction contract determines serving components, routing, storage, and scaling requirements.
The selected interaction contract determines serving components, routing, storage, and scaling requirements.
The selected interaction contract determines serving components, routing, storage, and scaling requirements.

values.label: Synchronous online serving
values.description: A caller submits a request and receives a prediction during the request interaction.

values.label: Asynchronous offline serving
values.description: Large collections are scored as batch jobs, with results retrieved after completion.

values.label: Push-based score delivery
values.description: Completed predictions are delivered to the caller through an independent notification.

values.label: Polling-based score retrieval

values.label: Broker-based completion notification
values.description: A message broker signals completion of offline scoring before consumers fetch results.

values.label: Model-version request routing

values.label: Cached offline predictions
values.description: Precomputed predictions are cached to reduce access latency for repeated or relevant requests.

values.label: Reduced fraud-response latency
values.description: Streaming and real-time decisioning reduce the elapsed time from suspicious transaction detection to account blocking.

values.label: Prediction-request feature payload
values.description: Including available contextual features directly in prediction requests.

clusters.name: Serving Architecture Style

values.label: Microservice architecture

values.label: Monolithic architecture
values.description: A monolithic serving architecture was considered as an alternative to decomposed ML integration and rejected.

values.label: Hybrid microservice-monolith architecture
values.description: Microservice and monolithic structures are combined when both separation and shared integration are needed.

values.label: Universal default monolith
values.description: Treating the standard monolith as suitable for every situation is explicitly rejected.

values.label: Weak ML component boundaries
values.description: ML components have weak boundaries that impede independent architecture and deployment.

values.label: Interleaved ML model dependencies
values.description: One model consumes another model's outputs, creating coupled component dependencies.

values.label: Clustered queue-backed serving

values.label: Parallel stateless prediction pipelines

values.label: Web-service model deployment

values.label: Replaceable serving components

values.label: Feature-service independence

values.label: Distributed development enablement

values.label: Software development cost

values.label: Elastic serving scale

values.label: Performance-oriented serving

values.label: Scalable ML pipeline operation

values.label: Sub-10-millisecond scoring latency

values.label: Software scalability

values.label: Hosted model-serving infrastructure

saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes: evaluation-related codes, fairness and business-impact assessment, experimentation, monitoring, scaling, managed infrastructure, CI/CD, data partitioning, and pipeline orchestration can be absorbed by the existing evaluation, training, serving, infrastructure, monitoring, governance, and delivery dimensions. However, several relevant architectural axes are not explicitly represented. First, model artifact serialization and interoperability is a distinct decision involving framework-specific, portable, or device-specific formats; model governance records artifacts but does not capture the choice of serialization format. Second, high availability and automated failure recovery constitute a resilience and recovery decision not subsumed by serving scalability, infrastructure placement, or monitoring. Third, human review of uncertain predictions is a distinct human-in-the-loop serving decision. Fourth, the taxonomy does not capture whether feature transformations are shared between training and serving or independently reimplemented, despite the resulting consistency and drift risks. Finally, modular decomposition and reuse of pipeline functions, including repository-backed components, is a code and workflow-architecture decision distinct from merely automating or orchestrating pipeline execution. The fallback and reversion codes also expose a missing model-release resilience axis: whether serving fails over to, or rolls back to, a prior model version.

The taxonomy covers most codes: ingestion mechanisms fit Data Ingestion Mode; online, offline, and nearline serving fit Prediction Serving Interaction; containers, serverless, microservices, orchestration, and scalability fit Serving Architecture and Scalability or ML Delivery Automation; and monitoring, retraining, AutoML preprocessing, feature generation, model selection, and hyperparameter tuning are represented by existing dimensions. However, the taxonomy lacks a general data-storage architecture axis. It does not capture choices concerning storage media, database families, storage roles, transactional versus analytical orientation, or data models and schemas; these are distinct from ingestion mode, feature stores, model stores, and infrastructure placement. It also lacks an end-to-end solution-architecture pattern axis covering alternatives such as lambda, kappa, polyglot, and IoT-oriented architectures. The related decomposition of data platforms, ownership boundaries, and cross-platform SLAs is not represented by model governance or delivery automation. Finally, stable ensemble construction is a model-building choice that is not subsumed by evaluation, hyperparameter tuning, or automated model selection, which concern selecting or assessing candidates rather than deciding whether and how to combine models.

uncovered_concepts: Columnar or NoSQL storage for logged data
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes through existing dimensions for infrastructure placement, serving architecture, feature stores, monitoring, evaluation, automation, governance, storage, and training computation. However, several relevant concepts introduce axes that are not currently represented. First, comprehensive capture of online-learning inputs, prediction requests, predictions, replay data, and their persistence timing and storage technology constitute a distinct data-logging and retention decision; monitoring and lineage do not specify what operational data is recorded, when it becomes durable, or where it is stored. Second, selecting CPU, GPU, or FPGA for inference is a distinct serving-execution hardware decision, not merely a choice of serving topology or infrastructure location. Third, distributed versus centralized/parallel analytical processing is distinct from data storage architecture and from model-training parallelism, and is relevant to the data-processing portion of the ML workflow. Other codes are covered or are forces, outcomes, implementation details, or methodological choices within existing axes: edge versus web-service deployment can be represented under serving architecture/infrastructure placement; feature stores and atomic retrieval under serving architecture; train/test splitting and cross-validation under evaluation; data and experiment versioning under governance and lineage; human-loop configuration under operational monitoring; and automation, retraining, model selection, and deployment pipelines under delivery automation and training scheduling.

uncovered_concepts: Explicit problem specification and business objectives
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes: batch versus online training, scheduling, evaluation and hold-out testing, business-impact evaluation, model serialization including PMML/ONNX, serving modes, monitoring and decay detection, notebook use, feature/data validation, storage, CI/CD, orchestration, registries, feature stores, and MLOps automation. However, it lacks a clear dimension for ML problem framing and objective definition before implementation; business-impact evaluation captures assessment of an already-defined objective, not the decision of what problem and objectives to pursue. It also lacks a model or neural-architecture selection axis: algorithm-family choices such as linear models versus random forests and NAS search-space and search-strategy choices are not subsumed by evaluation, hyperparameter optimization, or training computation. Finally, it does not clearly capture the integration-contract axis for distributed ML components and MLOps tools: network communication, service-level interface agreements, custom API integration, and provider substitutability are distinct from merely choosing a microservice, monolith, serving API, or orchestration platform.

uncovered_concepts: All-parameter updates as one model-state change
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes through existing dimensions for ingestion, storage, feature engineering, training, serving, automation, governance, monitoring, and deployment. However, it lacks a distinct decision axis for ground-truth and label-construction strategy: data profiling and validation can check prepared data, but they do not capture how labels are defined, separated into meaningful categories, or produced through human/agent workflows. It also lacks an explicit axis for consistency and atomicity of mutable online model state; serving update control and model stores capture where models are stored or updated, but not whether updates use atomic replacement, locking, or all-parameter transactions to prevent partially updated states. Finally, model interpretability is mentioned as an evaluation concern, but the taxonomy does not capture the architectural choice of whether and how interpretability instrumentation is integrated into the ML system. The remaining codes are subsumed by existing dimensions, including CI/CD and continuous training, versioning and experiment tracking, containerized artifacts, feature computation modes, shadow/canary testing, monitoring and drift detection, human review, storage choices, and serving topologies.

The taxonomy covers individual batch, streaming, near-real-time, synchronous, asynchronous, and broker-based execution modes through Data Processing Latency Mode, Prediction Serving Interaction, and Serving Topology. However, it does not capture the higher-level architectural decision of how offline, nearline, and online computation regimes are jointly coordinated, including the event/data-distribution mechanism and the combination of signals or models across regimes. These are distinct from choosing an individual ingestion or serving mode. The taxonomy also includes ground-truth construction under Model Evaluation Criteria, but does not capture the upstream decision of how labels are acquired—manual creation, web-based labeling tooling, or outsourced labeling services. The remaining open codes are either values or forces already subsumed by existing dimensions, such as serving topology, delivery automation, training triggers, monitoring, governance, evaluation, deployment targets, and infrastructure placement.

Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: monitoring and drift remediation by Operational Monitoring Strategy; human review by that dimension's human-review values; notebook, infrastructure, and language choices by ML Infrastructure and Access Placement; serialization and serving-runtime choices by Model Artifact Representation and Serving Deployment Target; feature stores and preprocessing by Feature Engineering Tooling and Data Storage Architecture; and retraining, CI/CD, orchestration, validation, rollback, and experimentation by ML Delivery Automation, Training Trigger Policy, Pre-release Validation, Model Governance and Lineage, and related dimensions. However, the minibatch makes a distinct architectural decision about the deployment unit: deploying only a prediction model behind an API versus deploying an end-to-end ML pipeline that includes data preparation, retraining, validation, and model deployment. Existing dimensions capture how deployment is automated and where it runs, but not whether the deployed unit is a model or the broader pipeline. Product-level verification controls are outside the ML-system design space and are therefore ignored.

saturation_history.rationale: Most codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: containerized and serverless deployment fit Serving Deployment Arrangement and Serving Packaging and Runtime; orchestration, pipelines, CI/CD, AutoML, environments, experiment tracking, lineage, monitoring, rollout, and model exchange fit existing delivery, optimization, governance, monitoring, artifact, and serving dimensions. However, the minibatch reveals two clear architectural axes not explicitly represented. First, it distinguishes the composition of the MLOps toolchain—an integrated platform or suite versus a mosaic of specialized tools—with associated coordination and human-intervention trade-offs; this is different from the existing axis of automation degree. Second, it introduces the choice of ML lifecycle process model and methodology, including agile, lightweight, heavyweight Waterfall/V-Model, ASUM-DM, standardized task templates, and product-specific roadmaps. Existing delivery automation and organizational-reorganization dimensions do not capture this process-methodology axis without conflating process governance with technical automation or organizational change.

uncovered_concepts: Injectable split ratio and random seed
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes: monitoring practices and signals fit Operational Monitoring Strategy; latency, asynchronous messaging, scaling, recovery, batch/real-time execution, and service decomposition fit the serving dimensions; notebook choices fit ML Development Environment; validation, drift detection, retraining, packaging, feature stores, storage, and delivery automation are also represented. However, several relevant architectural axes are not captured without conflation. First, the taxonomy lacks an explicit ML operating-responsibility model distinguishing data-science-led, operations-owned, and cross-functional production monitoring and operation. Second, it does not clearly represent the MLOps infrastructure sourcing decision—custom-built/in-house, fully managed vendor platform, or hybrid—because infrastructure placement and delivery automation capture location and automation, not ownership or sourcing. Third, it lacks a distinct dataset-partitioning and segregation strategy covering sequential versus randomized splits, injectable/custom strategies, runtime strategy selection, configurable ratios and seeds, and label-inclusive versus label-exclusive retrieval. Finally, access control and information-governance architecture for data products and heterogeneous users is broader than the existing model-access authentication value and is not otherwise represented.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask distinguishable questions—for example, id 18 Training Trigger Policy differs from id 17 Training Execution Mode, and id 45 Model Evaluation Dataset Strategy differs from id 46 Model Evaluation Criteria and Instrumentation. However, several dimensions overlap. Id 7 ML Delivery Automation contains direct answers to id 18 and id 17, such as 7.4 Event-triggered model deployment and 7.21 Continuous model training; move trigger choices to id 18 and execution-mode choices to id 17, retaining only automation choices in id 7. Id 16 Data Storage Architecture mixes storage with processing and access choices: move 16.7 Distributed parallel analytics processing to id 40 and 16.8 Data access and query technology to the relevant processing/development dimension. Id 41 Training Update Algorithm overlaps id 23 Model Optimization Strategy through 41.6 Scalable algorithm architecture and 23.6 Automated algorithm and model selection; keep algorithm-family/architecture values in id 41 and selection/search values in id 23. Id 42 Candidate-Model Search Execution also overlaps id 25 Training Parallelization and Resilience through parallel execution; retain candidate-search ordering in id 42 and move general training parallelization to id 25. criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: All decision-bearing passages can be placed under at least one taxonomy dimension. Examples include s19_p09 under automated algorithm/model selection (23.6), AutoML automation (7.14/7.20), accuracy requirements (46.10), and model serialization (13.2/13.4); s15_p03 and s02_p03 under ingestion, processing, storage, and trigger choices (39, 40, 16, 18); s06_p14 and s22_p12 under CI/CD, testing, and readiness strategies (7, 24); s20_p03 and s23_p10 under monitoring, drift, retraining, and collaboration (9, 17, 18); and s12_p07 and s16_p07 under serving, storage, and architecture alternatives (5, 16, 29). Background or introductory material such as s11_p09 and s27_p01 does not discuss a distinct design decision and therefore does not count against coverage. No unplaceable decision-bearing passages or taxonomy changes were identified.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers many major decisions, including AutoML selection and accuracy requirements (s19_p09), online versus batch training, reproducibility, monitoring, serving styles, CI/CD, and model serialization. However, several explicitly adopted options are not named. Add "message-queue ingestion," "query-based ingestion," "API ingestion," and "change-data-capture ingestion" to dimension 39 (s15_p03); add unit, convergence, NaN/numerical-validity, artifact, integration, infrastructure-compatibility, prediction-API, load/performance, data-validation, predictive-target, and environment-specific deployment checks to dimension 24 (s06_p14); add anomaly detection, rule-based fraud detection, and product/user-verification mitigation values to the relevant model or serving decision dimensions (s10_p02); add immutable raw-data storage, dedicated per-dataset pipelines, and partitioned parallel ingestion to dimensions 16/39 (s02_p03); and add explicit accuracy, speed/latency, and user-engagement objective values to dimension 46 (s03_p02).
